title: Phase-change memory endurance and drift for neuromorphic computing
bottleneck: Phase-change memory is a leading candidate for analog in-memory computing, but two material problems persist: resistance drift, where the amorphous state's resistance creeps over time and corrupts stored analog weights, and limited endurance under the billions of write cycles neural-network training demands.
why_it_blocks: Neuromorphic computing promises orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains for AI inference, but it needs memory devices that hold precise analog values reliably. Drift and endurance are the material ceiling between promising prototypes and deployable accelerators.
current_state: New alloys such as CrTe3 show practically no resistance drift across wide temperature ranges, and superlattice structures have reached hundreds of millions of cycles with multibit states. Yet combining no-drift behavior, high endurance, and CMOS-compatible manufacturing in one device remains undone.
